analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to test and report the harms of the algorithms they use in life-changing decisions like jobs, credit, housing, and health care.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require companies above certain size thresholds — generally those with over $50 million in annual revenue or data on more than a million people — to run ongoing "impact assessments" of the automated systems they use when those systems affect critical decisions: employment, credit, housing, health care, education, utilities, and more. Companies would have to test whether the algorithms perform differently by race, sex, age, disability, or income, consult outside stakeholders, try to fix harms, and file summary reports with the Federal Trade Commission. The FTC would build a public, searchable repository of these systems, hire a Bureau of Technology with at least 50 technologists, and enforce the rules with help from state attorneys general. The bill has been referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has not moved since [S1][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose lives are shaped by automated decisions — renters screened by algorithms, job applicants ranked by hiring software, patients routed by health care algorithms, borrowers scored by credit models — would gain disclosure, testing for bias, a public registry of systems in use, and a documented way to contest decisions. Civil rights and consumer advocates, and the FTC itself, would gain new authority and staffing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers facing automated decisions about jobs, credit, housing

how_it_helps.text: Companies above size thresholds would have to continuously study the algorithms they use for critical decisions — in hiring, credit, housing, health care, insurance, education, and utilities — and document any negative impact on consumers.

Companies would be required to try to eliminate or fix any likely material negative impact the algorithm has on consumers, in a timely way, including by pulling the algorithm from the market if needed.
The bill would direct the FTC to check whether algorithms perform differently for people based on race, sex, age, disability, family status, income, or veteran status, and to document those findings.

The FTC would build a public, searchable repository of the algorithms companies report, so consumers and researchers could see what automated systems are being used on them and how to contest or appeal a decision.

The FTC would gain a new Bureau of Technology with at least 50 technologists plus 25 additional enforcement staff, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents to enforce the law.

analysis.who_pays: Large technology companies and any business over the bill's size thresholds that uses algorithms in consequential decisions would bear the cost of mandatory testing, documentation, stakeholder consultation, and annual reporting to the FTC, plus compliance with FTC regulations. The public also funds the new FTC Bureau of Technology and enforcement staff.

drawbacks.text: The heaviest compliance burden falls on large companies, and opponents could argue the reporting requirements are expensive paperwork that slows product development without directly prohibiting any harmful algorithm — the bill requires assessments and mitigation, not bans.

The full impact assessments are not public: the bill expressly says companies need not disclose them to the Commission or the public beyond a limited summary report, so the deepest documentation stays private [S2].

Regulations would not take effect until two years after they are written, and the writing itself is due two years after enactment — meaning up to four years before the rules bind companies, even if the bill became law [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a real but partial safeguard: companies would have to test whether their algorithms discriminate or cause harm, report to regulators, and fix or pull harmful systems, and consumers would gain a public registry and contestation pathways. The costs are real too: the heaviest compliance burden falls on large tech and AI-driven companies, the full impact assessments would be kept confidential from the public (only summaries go to the FTC), small firms and the FTC itself would bear added burden, and critics argue the paperwork-first approach does not directly ban any harmful algorithm. On balance the protections for people facing consequential automated decisions outweigh the compliance costs, but the bill's fate — referred to committee with no movement — means the benefits are currently hypothetical.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not acted on it, so it sits there with no path to a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 19, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history since the referral.

If it had advanced, it would have required the Federal Trade Commission to write rules within two years requiring large companies to assess the impact of their algorithms on critical decisions and to report annually to the FTC.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved it forward: large tech and AI-driven companies avoid the mandated testing, documentation, and reporting that the bill would impose on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, companies that avoid algorithmic scrutiny

for.name: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republicans have signed on; the bill sits with a Republican-majority committee that has taken no action on it.

industries.industry: Large tech platforms and AI developers
industries.note: The companies selling or deploying algorithmic decision systems above the bill's size thresholds would face mandatory testing, stakeholder consultation, documentation, and annual FTC reporting for every consequential algorithm, plus FTC enforcement. The bill does not ban their business model, but it imposes real compliance costs and exposes discriminatory or harmful systems to scrutiny.

industries.industry: Smaller algorithm users (under the size thresholds)
industries.note: Firms below the revenue and data thresholds are exempt from the mandatory requirements, though they may voluntarily file summary reports. This spares small businesses but also leaves consumers unprotected from harmful algorithms used by smaller employers, landlords, and lenders.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action since referral, and no indication Energy and Commerce plans a hearing or markup, the most likely path is that the bill stalls in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress, as most bills referred to committee do.
